target.title: Allow host-local APK media sends
target.body:
## Summary

- allow content-verified host-local `.apk` attachments through the existing safe-document gate
- recognize signed APKs from their complete ZIP directory without trusting the filename
- preserve dependency APK detection for bounded prefix callers
- keep MIME-to-`.apk` output naming separate from path-only MIME classification
- add targeted media/outbound tests and a docs note for the host-local APK case

## What Problem This Solves

This is a narrow follow-up to [#79658](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/79658).

`TXT`/`JSON`/`YAML`/`YML` are already covered there. A valid signed Android APK is a separate real-world outbound document type that the host-local media path still rejects. This PR allows the verified APK MIME through the existing host-read safe-document gate without restoring the removed certificate or PEM scope.

## Why This Change Was Made

`file-type@22.0.1` recognizes ordinary APK prefixes from `classes*.dex`, but signed APKs may be reported as JAR when `META-INF/MANIFEST.MF` appears first. The host-read boundary therefore verifies the complete ZIP central directory and requires both `AndroidManifest.xml` and `classes*.dex` before accepting the APK MIME.

The complete-file requirement is limited to the host-read security boundary. Shared prefix-buffer callers retain `file-type`'s positive APK result, while path-only `.apk` callers receive no MIME claim until bytes are available.

## User Impact

Agents with host-read capability can attach a structurally verified APK as a document. Renamed JARs and generic ZIPs remain rejected, streamed/downloaded prefix classification is preserved, and a filename alone cannot classify arbitrary content as an APK.

## Evidence

- Live Telegram proof from the behavior-equivalent pre-rebase head: a real signed APK was loaded through the host-local media path and received as the `pr-87349-signed-apk-proof.apk` document. See [the screenshot and proof comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/87349#issuecomment-5015075334).
- Exact current head `97d1369b26` passes 267 focused tests:
  - `packages/media-core/src/mime.test.ts` — 154 passed
  - `src/media/web-media.test.ts` — 36 passed
  - `src/infra/outbound/message-action-runner.media.test.ts` — 77 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:core` — passed
- `pnpm tsgo:test:packages` — passed
- targeted `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` — passed
- Dependency contract inspected directly in `file-type@22.0.1/source/detectors/zip.js`: APK detection stops on `classes*.dex`, while an earlier `META-INF/MANIFEST.MF` returns JAR.

target.title: fix(secrets): collect persona-level TTS provider SecretRefs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Persona-level TTS provider API keys were not collected as SecretRefs, and agent persona registry paths bound the wrong path segment as `providerId` (literal `providers` instead of `elevenlabs`). That breaks secrets plan/audit and runtime resolution for agent persona TTS keys.

Fixes #89607

## Summary

The secret collector walks `messages.tts.providers.*.apiKey` but did not walk `messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` or `agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey`. When a persona overrides the TTS provider config with a file-source SecretRef, the secret resolver never saw the ref, so the `apiKey` reached the plugin as an unresolved object instead of the actual key string. The plugin then reported `not configured`.

This fix:

- Adds persona-level provider iteration in `collectTtsApiKeyAssignments`
- Registers two new target paths in the secret target registry (`messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` and `agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey`)
- Extends `hasAgentRuntimeSecretRefs` / agent-runtime target sets to detect persona-level TTS refs (including global `messages.tts.personas.*`)
- Fixes registry `providerId` binding so persona paths resolve to the provider key (e.g. `elevenlabs`)
- Adds regression coverage for top-level, persona-level, nested, empty-persona, and agent-level persona paths

Closes #89607

## Evidence

Live OpenClaw CLI on branch head with an isolated config that uses file-source SecretRefs for persona TTS keys: `secrets audit` reports `status: clean` with the persona paths collected and resolved; `infer tts convert --local` resolves those SecretRefs locally and reaches the ElevenLabs HTTP API (401 invalid key with a dummy secret, which proves resolution instead of the pre-fix `not configured` failure). Full capture in Real behavior proof.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Persona-level TTS provider SecretRefs under `messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` and `agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` must be collected, audited, and resolved so TTS conversion receives a string API key rather than an unresolved SecretRef object.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS 26.5.2, Node v26.5.0, OpenClaw branch `fix/tts-persona-secretref` at `/tmp/oc-89636` commit `ffc895b2f09` (OpenClaw 2026.7.2). - **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

  Step 1. Configured `messages.tts.providers`, `messages.tts.personas.narrator.providers`, and `agents.list[0].tts.personas.narrator.providers` with file SecretRefs (`source: file`, `provider: default`, `id: /elevenlabsNarratorKey`) and a matching JSON secrets file.

  Step 2. Audited secret collection and resolvability:

  ```bash
  export OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=/tmp/oc-proof-state-89636/openclaw.json
  export OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=/tmp/oc-proof-state-89636/state
  node scripts/run-node.mjs secrets audit --json
  ```

  Step 3. Ran local TTS conversion so runtime resolution must supply the persona/provider key:

  ```bash
  node scripts/run-node.mjs infer tts convert --local \
    --text 'hello proof' --json --output /tmp/proof-89636-tts.wav
  ```

- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output from the patched CLI:

  Secrets audit (persona file SecretRefs collected and resolvable):

  ```console
  $ node scripts/run-node.mjs secrets audit --json
  {
    "version": 1,
    "status": "clean",
    "resolution": {
      "refsChecked": 2,
      "skippedExecRefs": 0,
      "resolvabilityComplete": true
    },
    "filesScanned": [
      "/tmp/oc-proof-state-89636/openclaw.json"
  ```

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Claude CLI JSONL assistant records with the documented partial marker (`stop_reason: null`) were not relayed as streaming deltas, so WebChat/TUI waited for the full response instead of showing progressive text.

Fixes #86050

## Summary

Relay Claude CLI assistant records as streaming deltas so progressive output appears instead of waiting for the full response.

**Fix 1**: Parse `assistant` records from the Claude CLI JSONL stream and forward their text content as `chat.delta` events.

**Fix 2**: Gate on `stop_reason` using a positive partial signal: only forward records where `stop_reason` is explicitly present and `null` (the documented Claude CLI partial marker). Complete messages with `stop_reason: "end_turn"` are skipped to avoid duplicating the final message. Records without `stop_reason` at all are ignored as ambiguous (could be complete messages from custom `claude-stream-json` backends).

**Fix 3** (rank-up): When commentary classification is active, assistant-record partials buffer into `pendingClaudeText` like stream_event text so pre-tool narration does not land on final assistant deltas.

### Changed files

- `src/agents/cli-output.ts` -- `parseClaudeCliPartialAssistantDelta` with positive `stop_reason: null` guard; commentary routing for assistant partials
- `src/agents/cli-output.test.ts` -- partial forwarding, complete-message skip, absent-stop_reason rejection, commentary classification regression

## Evidence

Live Claude CLI `stream-json` session produced a real assistant record with `stop_reason: null`. The production `createCliJsonlStreamingParser` on this branch head relayed that record as a streaming delta. Full terminal capture is in Real behavior proof below.

target.title: feat(gateway): allow chat.inject to override provider attribution via originAgent
target.body:
## Summary

Adds an optional `originAgent` field to `ChatInjectParamsSchema` and persists it as a **separate, dedicated attribution field** on the injected assistant transcript entry. The pre-existing `(provider: "openclaw", model: "gateway-injected")` sentinel pair is **preserved unchanged**, so the runtime replay filter at `src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/replay-history.ts:271` continues to correctly drop these rows from being replayed back to the next model call.

UI avatar/handle resolvers can key off the new persisted `originAgent` field to render the true source of a cross-agent inject (e.g. Hermes, Codex) instead of always showing the OpenClaw avatar.

## Why

`chat.inject` is the canonical RPC for cross-agent transcript writes. Today the persisted entry has `provider: "openclaw"` hard-coded, with `additionalProperties: false` on the schema closing the door on any caller-supplied attribution. When external agents (Hermes, Codex, Claude Code, etc.) inject via this RPC, the message renders with OpenClaw's avatar and the only visible attribution is whatever the caller embeds in body text. This breaks the "who said what" guarantee in long transcripts.

Discovered in production by an external agent (Hermes) attempting a cross-agent verify ping into a webchat session. The body-tag workaround ("FROM: Hermes —") works at-a-glance but degrades attribution clarity over time and across many entries.

## Behavior

- **With `originAgent` set:** persisted entry gets a new `originAgent: "<value>"` field. `provider` and `model` are unchanged.
- **Without `originAgent`:** behavior is byte-identical to current main. No new field is written. Fully backward compatible.
- **Empty / whitespace-only input:** schema rejects literal `""` (`minLength: 1`); persistence helper additionally trims whitespace and treats blanks as absent, so a malformed value never lands on disk even if a future schema change loosens validation.

## Why a separate field, not provider override

The Codex review on the prior commit caught a real correctness defect: `provider` is part of the runtime replay contract, not just display. `normalizeAssistantReplayContent` (`src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/replay-history.ts:271`) drops gateway-injected rows from model replay only when `provider === "openclaw"` and the model is one of `{ "delivery-mirror", "gateway-injected" }`. Overwriting `provider` would have caused transcript-only injects to leak into model context, duplicating content and risking provider ordering rejections.

The redesigned patch keeps the sentinel pair untouched and adds attribution as a dedicated parallel field. UI consumers read the new field; the replay filter is unaffected.

## Security

`chat.inject` is already gated at operator-privilege scope (`src/gateway/method-scopes.ts`). Anyone who can call it can already write arbitrary assistant content into a session transcript. `originAgent` is **purely presentational** and introduces no new impersonation surface beyond what current authorized callers already possess. Because the sentinel pair is preserved, the previously-flagged security risk (UI-only injects entering model replay) does not apply to this revision.

## Files

- `src/gateway/protocol/schema/logs-chat.ts` — schema field with `minLength: 1`, `maxLength: 100`
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.ts` — handler param + helper threading
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat-transcript-inject.ts` — new persisted field, sentinel preserved, trim+empty normalization
- `apps/shared/OpenClawKit/Sources/OpenClawProtocol/GatewayModels.swift` — regenerated via `pnpm protocol:gen:swift`

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** Cross-agent `chat.inject` calls render with the OpenClaw avatar in the operator's webchat UI because the persisted assistant entry has no caller-controlled attribution field. External agents currently have no way to mark the inject as their own without putting "FROM: Hermes —" inline in body text, which degrades transcript clarity. This patch adds a dedicated `originAgent` persisted field while preserving the `(provider: "openclaw", model: "gateway-injected")` sentinel that the replay-history filter relies on.

**Real environment tested:** Sandboxed checkout of openclaw main at `/tmp/openclaw-pr/openclaw-fresh` with the patched files and the regenerated protocol bindings. Used the actual openclaw runtime — `appendInjectedAssistantMessageToTranscript` and `validateChatInjectParams` are invoked via `node` through `tsx` against synthetic transcript fixtures created with the project's own `createTranscriptFixtureSync` helper. No mocks, no stubs, no real session keys, no production data.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```
node node_modules/.bin/tsx scripts/proof-chat-inject-origin-agent.mts
node node_modules/.bin/tsx scripts/proof-chat-inject-schema.mts
```

Both scripts are committed under `scripts/` in this PR so a maintainer can rerun them.

**Evidence after fix:** Live stdout captured from the runtime invocations above. Persistence-layer output shows the actual `provider`, `model`, and `originAgent` fields read back from the jsonl transcript file on disk after the patched code wrote to it. Schema-layer output is the AJV validator's verdict on real input shapes.

## What Problem This Solves

`sessions.create` with `parentSessionKey` (fork or non-fork) performs no plugin-ownership check against the source session, letting a write-scoped plugin runtime fork or link to any other plugin's session and read its full transcript or inherit its metadata. `sessions.delete` already enforces this check via `rejectPluginRuntimeDeleteMismatch`; `sessions.create` does not.

target.title: fix(media): apply SSRF guard to byteplus and runway generated video downloads
target.body:
Closes #103083

## What Problem This Solves..

Fixes an issue where the `byteplus` and `runway` bundled video-generation providers fetch the generated-video bytes from a URL taken directly out of the provider's own JSON completion response, using an unguarded download call that never re-applies the SSRF guard (DNS pinning, private/loopback/link-local address blocking) that the same providers already apply to their submit and poll requests.

If the upstream provider API is compromised, MITM'd, or configured with a malicious custom base URL, it can set the result URL to an internal address (for example `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...` or `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/admin`) and OpenClaw will connect to it and save the response bytes as the generated video attachment. This is the agent-tool video-generation path (`src/agents/tools/video-generate-tool.ts`), reachable with default configuration and no `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` opt-in. CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery).

The guarded siblings `fal`, `google`, and `openrouter` already re-apply the SSRF guard to this exact "download the URL the JSON body told us to fetch" step, and `minimax` (#102072) and `xai` (#104836) were fixed the same way after #103083 was filed. `byteplus` and `runway` were simply never updated. `vydra` shares the gap but is already covered by open PR #105884, so it is intentionally out of scope here.

## Why This Change Was Made

Root cause: `downloadBytePlusVideo` and `downloadRunwayVideos` bottom out in `fetchProviderDownloadResponse`, which calls a bare `fetchWithTimeout` with no DNS pinning and no private-network block, and the resolved `allowPrivateNetwork` / `dispatcherPolicy` were never threaded into the download step even though both providers resolve them for submit and poll.

The fix has two parts:

1. Add one canonical guarded download helper, `fetchGuardedProviderDownloadResponse`, in `src/media-understanding/shared.ts` (exported from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/provider-http`). It mirrors `fetchProviderDownloadResponse` (same download-stage retry, deadline, and body-timeout semantics) but always routes through the SSRF guard, so private/loopback/link-local result URLs are blocked by default. Unlike the earlier closed attempts (#102096, #102134, #108267) it does not gate the guard behind `if (allowPrivateNetwork || dispatcherPolicy)`, which left the default-configuration gap open.

2. Thread the operator's configured request policy (`models.providers.<id>.request`) into `resolveProviderHttpRequestConfig` for both providers, matching the merged `minimax` and `xai` fixes. Previously these calls hard-coded `allowPrivateNetwork: false` (byteplus) or omitted the request config (runway), so the resolved `allowPrivateNetwork` / `dispatcherPolicy` were always defaults. Without this, an operator who intentionally points a provider at a private endpoint would have their legitimate private artifact URL blocked by the new guard with no escape hatch. The resolved policy is now honored consistently for submit, poll, and download, and is passed into the guarded download.

Boundary: the change stays at the provider download boundary plus one shared helper; submit/poll transport is unchanged in shape. `minimax` and `xai` are already guarded, and `vydra` is covered by #105884, so no sibling is left one-sided by this PR.

## User Impact

Generated-video downloads for `byteplus` and `runway` now refuse to connect to private, loopback, or link-local addresses by default, closing the SSRF exposure when a provider response is attacker-influenced. Operators who intentionally point these providers at a private endpoint keep working by setting the existing `models.providers.<id>.request.allowPrivateNetwork` / request-policy options, exactly as they already do for other providers; that opt-in now flows through to the download step. No configuration changes are required for the common (public provider) case.

## Evidence

Real before/after, driving the actual production download helpers against a real loopback HTTP server, with the real SSRF guard code (`src/infra/net/fetch-guard.ts`, `src/infra/net/ssrf.ts`) unmodified. `fetchProviderDownloadResponse` is the download helper `byteplus` and `runway` call on `origin/main` (5ca5c5c); `fetchGuardedProviderDownloadResponse` is the helper this patch routes them through. Driven at head `06fd7cd227` on identical loopback input:

```
BEFORE main-path fetchProviderDownloadResponse (default config) -> url=http://127.0.0.1:41733/secret-metadata server_hits=["/secret-metadata"] downloaded_bytes=LEAKED-INTERNAL-BYTES-9f3c2a
AFTER patched-path fetchGuardedProviderDownloadResponse (default config) -> url=http://127.0.0.1:37263/secret-metadata server_hits=[] rejected_with=Blocked hostname or private/internal/special-use IP address
AFTER patched-path fetchGuardedProviderDownloadResponse (allowPrivateNetwork opt-in) -> url=http://127.0.0.1:38295/secret-metadata server_hits=["/secret-metadata"] downloaded_bytes=LEAKED-INTERNAL-BYTES-9f3c2a
```

With default configuration the old helper connected to the attacker-supplied loopback address and returned its bytes as the video buffer; the patched helper never opened a socket to the loopback server (`server_hits=[]`) and rejected with the guard's blocked-hostname error before any connection. With the operator's `allowPrivateNetwork` opt-in the patched helper downloads the private URL exactly as before, confirming the escape hatch works.

What was not driven live: no real cloud-metadata service or non-loopback private address was contacted (only a loopback stand-in), and the provider submit/poll requests were not exercised against a live provider API.

target.title: fix(mcp): bind stored OAuth refresh token to its issuer
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a remote MCP server configured with `auth: "oauth"` could cause OpenClaw to hand a previously stored refresh token to a different authorization server than the one that issued it.

When such a server answers an authenticated request with `401 Unauthorized` and a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="..."` challenge that points at a new Protected Resource Metadata document, OpenClaw lets the MCP SDK rediscover the authorization server from that document and then refresh the still-exposed stored credential. If the new metadata names a different issuer, the stored refresh token is POSTed to that issuer's `token_endpoint`. A server that can influence its own `WWW-Authenticate` header (or a network position that can rewrite it) can therefore harvest a refresh token that was minted for an entirely different authorization server.

## Why This Change Was Made

Stored MCP OAuth credentials had no record of which authorization-server issuer produced them, so nothing bound a refresh token to its issuer across a discovery change. This change persists the issuing authorization server alongside the refresh token and refuses to expose that token to the SDK once discovery selects a different issuer, forcing an interactive reauthorization instead. It deliberately uses issuer-bound provenance rather than a same-origin requirement between the MCP endpoint and its authorization server, because RFC 9728 explicitly allows a protected resource to advertise an externally hosted authorization server.

## User Impact

Refresh tokens for OAuth MCP servers are now only ever sent to the authorization server that issued them. A `resource_metadata` challenge that redirects discovery to a new issuer no longer silently replays the old refresh token; the connection reports that it requires authorization (`openclaw mcp login <server>`) instead. Legitimate deployments whose metadata moves but keeps the same issuer continue to refresh without interruption, and normal same-issuer refresh is unchanged.

## Why this is the right boundary

The MCP OAuth credential provider (`src/agents/mcp-oauth-provider.ts`) already owns every read and write of the stored token through the SDK's `OAuthClientProvider`. Binding provenance there means the guard sits on the single seam the SDK calls (`tokens()`) to obtain the refresh token, so no SDK code path can reach the credential without passing the issuer check. The challenge handler in `src/agents/mcp-oauth.ts` and the persisted shape in `src/agents/mcp-oauth-store.ts` are the matching owners for capturing and validating that provenance. No sibling surface refreshes MCP OAuth tokens: the auth-profile path (`src/agents/mcp-auth-profile.ts`) refreshes provider profiles, not MCP server credentials, and does not touch this store.

The stored field is an additive optional value inside the existing `store_json` column, so there is no SQLite schema-version bump; older readers ignore it. Tokens whose discovery state is present get their issuer snapshotted from it before a discovery-changing challenge drops it. Token-only rows imported by Doctor (`src/infra/state-migrations.mcp-oauth-format.ts` accepts `tokens` without `discoveryState`) have no recoverable issuer, so the provider fails closed: once discovery has run and no validated provenance matches, the refresh token is withheld from the SDK and the connection asks for a one-time reauthorization rather than replaying the credential against the newly selected issuer.

## Verification

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/mcp-oauth-refresh-issuer.test.ts src/agents/mcp-oauth-refresh.test.ts src/agents/mcp-oauth.test.ts src/agents/mcp-oauth-fetch.test.ts` -> 4 files, 40 passed.

- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` and `oxfmt --check` clean on the four changed files.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json` clean.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: an OAuth MCP server's `401` + new `resource_metadata` challenge caused the stored refresh token to be sent to a different authorization-server issuer than the one that issued it, both for provenance-bound tokens and for token-only rows imported by Doctor.
Real environment tested: drove the real production fetch wrapper `withMcpOAuthBearer` from `src/agents/mcp-oauth-fetch.ts` (which calls the real `resolveMcpOAuthAccessToken`, the real MCP SDK `auth()`, and the real SQLite-backed credential provider) against a fresh `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, on pristine main `9061aa8ea8` and on the patched tree. The stored credential, the SDK discovery/refresh flow, and the on-disk state stayed real; only the HTTP fetch was replaced by an in-process origin that plays the MCP server, the relocated metadata document (`https://metadata.example/pr-metadata`), the new issuer's metadata, and its token endpoint. Two seeded states were exercised: (A) a token whose discovery names `https://auth-old.example`, and (B) a token-only row with no discovery, both hit by a `401` steering discovery to `https://auth-new.example`.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: for each seed, issue one `POST https://mcp.example.com/mcp` through `withMcpOAuthBearer`; the server replies `401` with `resource_metadata="https://metadata.example/pr-metadata"`, whose document names issuer `https://auth-new.example`, and observe whether `refresh_token=stored-refresh-secret` reaches `https://auth-new.example/token`.
Evidence after fix:
```
# BEFORE (pristine main 9061aa8ea8, identical inputs)
[A] provenance-bound token, challenge redirects to new issuer:
  outcome                    : retry HTTP 200
```

target.title: fix(googlechat): surface reply send failures instead of silently dropping chunks
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`deliverGoogleChatReply` (extensions/googlechat/src/monitor-reply-delivery.ts:79-109 on `main`) wrapped every chunk send in a try/catch that only logged the error and kept looping. Two silent-loss paths resulted:

1. A failing `sendGoogleChatMessage` for any non-first chunk was logged and the chunk was dropped; the loop continued and the function resolved normally.
2. When the first-chunk typing-message update failed and the fallback resend also failed, that second failure was logged and swallowed too — the entire reply was lost.

The core reply dispatcher contract treats a rejected `deliver` as a failed delivery and a resolved one as visible delivery: `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts:476-483` awaits `options.deliver(...)` and only routes to `onError` / `failed-deliver` in `.catch`. Resolving after a swallowed send error therefore reported the turn as delivered while the user saw nothing (or only part of the reply).

## Why This Change Was Made

Restructure the chunk loop so the typing-update fallback stays, but any final send failure rejects out of `deliverGoogleChatReply`, matching the dispatcher contract. The typing-update catch is kept because a stale typing placeholder is recoverable — the same chunk is immediately resent as a new message, and only that resend failing is a real delivery failure. This mirrors the LINE sibling, which documents that a lost bubble "must surface as a partial delivery, not silent success" (extensions/line/src/auto-reply-delivery.ts:217-219), and the same-channel precedent https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/96646 ("throw on non-ok instead of parsing error body as success").

Fix classification: channel delivery error-propagation fix, additive behavior change only on the failure path; no config, SDK, or core changes.

## User Impact

- Google Chat reply send failures now surface through the dispatcher `onError` path instead of being counted as visible deliveries, so dropped or partially delivered replies are no longer reported as successfully sent.
- The existing typing-fallback behavior is unchanged when the resend succeeds.

## Evidence

### Integration-backed failure-path proof (real HTTP stack, loopback stub)

New committed regression test `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.reply-delivery-failure.test.ts` drives the production stack end to end against a local HTTP impersonator of the Google Chat API: `deliverGoogleChatReply` → `sendGoogleChatMessage` → `withGoogleChatResponse` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → real `google-auth-library` JWT signing and token exchange. Only global `fetch` is stubbed (rerouting `chat.googleapis.com` / `oauth2.googleapis.com` to `127.0.0.1`); the service-account key is a throwaway RSA key generated in-process, the stub issues the token, and the stub answers the second `spaces.messages` create with a real HTTP 500 error envelope. The deliver/onError wiring mirrors `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.ts:408-429`, and the outcome labels follow the dispatcher contract in `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts:476-483`. No real credentials, endpoints, or user data anywhere.

Standalone transcript of the same flow (three-chunk reply, second create → 500), after the fix:

```
stub: POST /token (grant=jwt-bearer) -> 200 access_token=ya29.stub-token (redacted)
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #1 text="First chunk of the assistant reply." -> 200
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #2 text="Second chunk of the assistant reply." -> 500
runtime.error: [default] Google Chat text reply failed: Error: Google Chat API 500: {"error":{"code":500,"message":"stub: backend unavailable","status":"INTERNAL"}}
dispatcher: deliveryOutcome=failed-deliver
summary: tokenExchanges=1 messageCreates=2 createStatuses=[200,500] patchAttempts=0 onErrorCalls=1
```

Same stub, same input, pre-fix `monitor-reply-delivery.ts` from `origin/main` (reverse control): the 500 is logged and swallowed, the third chunk is still sent, and the dispatcher records the reply as delivered with `onError` never firing:

```
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #1 text="First chunk of the assistant reply." -> 200
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #2 text="Second chunk of the assistant reply." -> 500
runtime.error: Google Chat message send failed: Error: Google Chat API 500: {"error":{"code":500,...}}
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #3 text="Third chunk of the assistant reply." -> 200
dispatcher: deliveryOutcome=delivered
summary: tokenExchanges=1 messageCreates=3 createStatuses=[200,500,200] patchAttempts=0 onErrorCalls=0
```

Second after-fix scenario (typing placeholder already deleted upstream: `PATCH .../messages/typing` → 404, resend create → 500): the recoverable placeholder failure is logged, the resend failure rejects and reaches `onError`:

```
stub: PATCH /v1/spaces/AAA/messages/typing -> 404 (typing placeholder gone)
runtime.error: Google Chat message send failed: Error: Google Chat API 404: {"error":{"code":404,...}}
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #1 text="First chunk of the assistant reply." -> 500
runtime.error: [default] Google Chat text reply failed: Error: Google Chat API 500: {"error":{"code":500,...}}
dispatcher: deliveryOutcome=failed-deliver
summary: tokenExchanges=1 messageCreates=1 createStatuses=[500] patchAttempts=1 onErrorCalls=1
```

| | BEFORE (`origin/main` source) | AFTER (this PR) |
|---|---|---|
| Stub observed | 3 real `POST .../messages` (`[200,500,200]`) | 2 real `POST .../messages` (`[200,500]`), third chunk never attempted |
| `deliver` result | resolved — reply counted delivered, chunk 2 silently dropped | rejected with `Google Chat API 500: {...}` |
| Dispatcher outcome | `delivered`, `onError` never fires | `failed-deliver`, `onError` fires once with the API error |
| New integration test | 2 of 3 tests fail (reverse-verified) | 3/3 pass |

### Before vs after (same regression tests, same mocks)

| Scenario | `origin/main` | this PR |

| Non-first chunk send rejects | resolves; chunk dropped, loop continues | rejects with the send error |
| Typing update fails, fallback resend rejects | resolves; whole reply lost | rejects with the resend error |
| Typing update fails, fallback resend succeeds | resends, resolves (kept) | resends, resolves (unchanged) |

### Contract chain (source verified on `main`)

| Layer | File | Line | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Channel deliver | `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.ts` | 408-421 | `deliver: async (payload) => { await deliverGoogleChatReply(...) }` |
| Channel onError | `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.ts` | 425-429 | `[accountId] Google Chat <kind> reply failed: <err>` |

| Dispatcher contract | `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts` | 476-483 | `await options.deliver(...)`; only `.catch` routes to `onError` / `failed-deliver` |
| Sibling precedent | `extensions/line/src/auto-reply-delivery.ts` | 217-219 | lost bubble must surface as partial delivery, not silent success |

### Control-red (reverse verification)

Reverting only `monitor-reply-delivery.ts` to `origin/main` while keeping the new tests:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.reply-delivery-failure.test.ts

```

### Test suite

### What was not tested

- A real Google Chat workspace send (requires live service-account credentials); the loopback impersonator covers the full production HTTP/auth/guard stack instead, including the real error-envelope parsing that builds the `Google Chat API 500: ...` message.

target.title: fix(auto-reply): defer rollover for legacy pending-reset tombstones with active runs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`initSessionState` protects live transcripts from implicit rollover with `deferImplicitRolloverForActiveRun` (`src/auto-reply/reply/session.ts:689`): when a stale session still has an active reply run, the rollover is deferred so the transcript is never renamed out from under the running writer ("Implicit daily/idle rollover must not rename a transcript while that exact session's active writer is still running").

#111140 (disable automatic session resets by default) added an early return to `evaluateSessionFreshness` for the legacy `updatedAt === 0` pending-reset tombstone (`src/config/sessions/reset-policy.ts:88-91`), yielding `{ fresh: false }` **without** a `staleReason`. The deferral guard additionally requires `entryFreshness.staleReason != null` (`session.ts:694`) — a condition that was always true before #111140, when `updatedAt: 0` flowed through the daily/idle evaluation and came out stale with `staleReason: "daily"` under the old default. Post-#111140 the condition is never true for tombstoned entries, so the active-run deferral is silently skipped for exactly those sessions and the live transcript is archived mid-write.

Failure scenario: a user on a prior release has a session with the `updatedAt: 0` pending-reset marker (acknowledged shipped state — the reset-policy comment says "Older releases persisted updatedAt=0 as an explicit pending reset marker") and a reply run still active in that session. The next inbound message evaluates freshness → tombstone → `fresh: false`, no `staleReason` → deferral skipped → `<sessionId>.jsonl` is renamed to `.jsonl.reset.<ts>` while the run is still writing; the run's remaining output is split/lost across the rollover boundary. This regresses both the new `none` default and explicitly configured `daily`/`idle` policies.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `staleReason != null` condition encoded a pre-#111140 invariant (`fresh === false` ⇒ a stale reason exists) that the tombstone branch broke. Removing the condition restores the guard for every `fresh === false` entry; the tombstone carries the same live-transcript invariant the guard exists to protect. The alternative (inventing a `staleReason` for the tombstone) would mislabel the reset end reason downstream, and #111140's own test codifies the bare `{ fresh: false }` shape, so the guard site is the right place to fix.

## User Impact

Before: upgrading users with legacy pending-reset tombstones can have an active session's transcript rotated away mid-run when the next message arrives — remaining model output lands in an archived/orphaned transcript. After: tombstoned sessions with an active run defer rollover exactly like daily/idle-stale sessions; the rollover happens once the run completes.

## Evidence

- New regression test `defers rollover of a legacy pending-reset tombstone while the same session has an active run` in `src/auto-reply/reply/session.test.ts` — clones the existing `defers implicit daily rollover while the same session has an active run` harness with `updatedAt: 0`. **Fails on current main** (`isNewSession === true`, transcript archived), passes with the fix.
- Full file suite: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/session.test.ts` → 141/141 pass, including the pre-existing deferral tests (daily stale, queued-reservation exclusion), confirming the guard's other behaviors are unchanged.
- Sibling suite: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/sessions/reset-policy.test.ts` → pass (#111140's codified `{ fresh: false }` tombstone contract untouched).
- Introduced-by: #111140; pre-change behavior verified at `git show e23dde3de5^:src/config/sessions/reset-policy.ts` (no tombstone early return; `updatedAt: 0` evaluated stale with `staleReason: "daily"`).

## Real behavior proof (added after review)

Live runs of the real `initSessionState` (no mocks of the changed surface) with a real on-disk store/transcript and a real `replyRunRegistry` active run, on head `fd185f253c` vs main `2e8b042f9f`:

- **Before**: tombstone + active run → `isNewSession=true`, live transcript archived mid-run (`archives=1`, `transcriptIntact=false`), new session id minted — the race the deferral guard exists to prevent.
- **After**: same setup → `isNewSession=false`, transcript intact, zero archives while the run is active; after the run completes, the identical tombstone rolls over normally (`isNewSession=true`, `archives=1`) — deferred while active, not swallowed.

target.title: fix(channels): preserve terminal ingress outcomes when stop abort races delivery return
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`createChannelIngressMonitor` (introduced in #111186, extended in #111249) rewrites a delivery's outcome to `failed-retryable` whenever the monitor's stop abort races the delivery's return — checked *before* the result is inspected at `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor.ts:327`. This discards two terminal/handoff outcomes:

1. **`completed`**: the channel finished its side effects and reported success, but the claim is settled as failed-retryable and released for retry. On restart the row replays and the message is delivered a second time.
2. **`deferred`** (explicit result or `onDeferred`/`onAdoptionFinalizing`/`onAbandoned` handoff): the claim is released for retry even though a deferred owner (reply lane / agent run / debounce flush) still owns it — the deferred owner completes its work *and* the released row replays.

The drain contract this contradicts is explicit in `src/channels/message/ingress-drain.ts:623-635`: "a terminal completed/failed result still settles even if abort raced the return", and a genuine `deferred` result under abort is left unsettled for its owner (:629-635, :642-645). The monitor's rewrite prevents both behaviors from ever reaching the drain.

Reproduced with a focused test: a delivery that returns `{kind: "completed"}` after `monitor.stop()` aborts it lands in `queue.listPending()` with `lastError: "Channel ingress monitor is stopped."` — released for a duplicate replay — instead of settling terminal.

## Why This Change Was Made

#111186/#111249 migrated six channels onto the shared monitor, so every migrated channel (Signal, Slack, Discord, iMessage, Twitch, Tlon) inherits this race on every gateway stop/restart with an in-flight delivery — the exact duplicate-delivery scenario the durability work is designed to prevent.

The fix reorders the outcome checks so terminal (`completed`, `failed-retryable`) and handoff (`deferred`, `deferredHandoff`) outcomes pass through to the drain first; the abort→`failed-retryable` conversion now applies only to void returns with no handoff, where the work state is genuinely unknown and retry is the safe choice. That preserves the existing "releases a pre-adoption delivery for retry before disposing on stop" behavior (still covered by its test).

## User Impact

Before: any channel stop/restart that aborts an in-flight delivery after the channel already completed (or deferred) the work can deliver that message again after restart — duplicate user-visible messages on the migrated channels. After: completed work settles terminal and deferred claims stay with their owner; only truly unfinished work is retried.

## Evidence

- New regression tests in `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor.test.ts`:
  - `completes deliveries whose terminal result races a stop abort` — **fails on current main** (row lands in `listPending()` with `lastError: "Channel ingress monitor is stopped."`), passes with the fix.
  - `keeps deferred handoffs with their owner when a stop abort races the return` — fails on current main (claim released instead of staying with its owner), passes with the fix.
- Full sibling suite: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/channels/message/` → 22 files, 285/285 pass, including the pre-existing stop/abort tests (`releases a pre-adoption delivery for retry before disposing on stop`, `stops with an outstanding deferred claim without waiting for adoption`) which confirm the void-return retry path is unchanged.
- Channel-level suites for the migrated channels: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/twitch/src/twitch-ingress.test.ts extensions/signal/src/signal-ingress.test.ts extensions/line/src/webhook-spool.test.ts` → all pass.
- Introduced-by: #111186 (this code is <48h old on main); the abort-ordering interacts with every channel just migrated in #111186/#111249.

## Real behavior proof (added after review)

Live stop/restart runs against the real durable ingress queue (SQLite state dir) + real monitor/drain, no mocks of the changed surface, on head `3493240a83` vs main `2e8b042f9f` (same `src/channels/message/` code):

- **Completed + stop-abort race**: before — row released (`pending=1`, `"Channel ingress monitor is stopped."`) and the restart monitor replays it (`side-effect:evt-1` + `REPLAY:evt-1` = duplicate); after — terminal settle (`claims=0 pending=0`), no replay.
- **Deferred + stop-abort race**: before — claim released from its owner at stop; when a reload monitor starts before the owner finishes, the row replays and the owner's late `queue.complete` returns `false` (claim stolen). After — claim retained (`claims=1`), owner completes with its CAS claim token, restart replays nothing.
- Deferred claims whose owner dies without completing still recover via the drain's stale-claim lease checks — intended at-least-once, unchanged.

target.title: fix(channels): keep healthy accounts' message actions when one credential SecretRef fails
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When one channel account's credential is an unresolved SecretRef (for example an env-provider ref whose variable is missing), the whole channel's message actions silently disappear from the agent `message` tool — including the actions of every healthy account on that channel.

Root cause: account enumeration in the googlechat, slack, zalo, and mattermost plugins resolved every account's credentials **strictly**. One broken account threw, and core's `describeMessageToolSafely` (`src/channels/plugins/message-action-discovery.ts:104-118`) caught the throw and returned `null` for the entire channel, so healthy accounts were collateral damage. The feishu plugin already avoids this: its read-only account resolution uses `baseMode: "inspect"` (`extensions/feishu/src/accounts.ts:337-346`), where an unresolved ref reads as "not configured" and the enumeration simply skips that account.

This is the plugin-side completion of [#109766](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109766) ("keep healthy channel accounts running when one credential fails"), which established per-account isolation at the gateway/secret-runtime layer; these four enumeration paths still defeated it at message-tool discovery time.

## Why This Change Was Made

Mirror the feishu inspect pattern in all four plugins, keeping the blast radius minimal:

- Account resolvers gain a `mode: "strict" | "inspect"` option (default `strict`, so every existing caller keeps today's behavior). In `inspect` mode an unresolved SecretRef reads as no credential, exactly like feishu's `baseMode: "inspect"`.
- Enumeration / discovery paths (`listEnabled*Accounts`, `describeMessageTool`, mattermost directory gating) pass `mode: "inspect"`, so one broken account degrades to "unconfigured" instead of throwing away the whole channel's tool schema.
- Direct single-account use (send, monitor, gateway startup) keeps strict resolution and still throws on unresolved refs — no silent credential fallback.
- zalo/mattermost already had a setup-only `allowUnresolvedSecretRef` boolean with identical semantics; it is renamed to the shared `mode: "strict" | "inspect"` switch (migrating its 3 setup call sites) so there is one canonical knob instead of two overlapping ones.
- slack's `isSlackInteractiveRepliesEnabled` runs inside `describeSlackMessageTool`; it gains the same optional mode so a broken default account cannot break schema building (its runtime send-path callers stay strict).

No core, SDK, config, or gateway changes; core's catch-all in `describeMessageToolSafely` stays as the generic safety net.

Fix classification: additive defensive isolation on fan-in discovery paths; no behavior change for healthy configs or for strict single-account use.

## User Impact

- A Slack/Google Chat/Zalo/Mattermost setup with several accounts no longer loses **all** of that channel's message actions (send/react/read/…) when one account's SecretRef cannot be resolved; the broken account alone drops out and remains visible to doctor/status per [#109766](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109766).
- One canonical `strict | inspect` resolution mode per plugin instead of a setup-only boolean plus implicit strict-everywhere behavior.

## Evidence

Base: `e57acb1d94312a7162debf300db9ba05702bd240` (`origin/main`) · Head: `6364c3af1635b90d6b43e192796e43131a541e27`

Config: two accounts per channel, `broken` = env-provider SecretRef pointing at a missing variable (the shape the gateway leaves in config), `healthy` = literal credential.

|---|---|---|
| `listEnabledGoogleChatAccounts` | THREW `Error: unresolved SecretRef` | OK — broken = `credentialSource "none"`, healthy = `inline` |
| `listEnabledSlackAccounts` | THREW `UnresolvedSecretInputError` | OK — broken = `botTokenSource "none"` |
| `listEnabledZaloAccounts` | THREW `UnresolvedSecretInputError` | OK — broken = `tokenSource "none"` |
| mattermost `describeMessageTool` | THREW `UnresolvedSecretInputError` | OK — `{actions:["send","react"]}` |
| feishu `listEnabledFeishuAccounts` (control) | OK `[healthy]` | OK `[healthy]` |

| core `discoveredActions.slack` | `[]` | `["send","react","reactions","read","edit","delete","download-file","upload-file","pin","unpin","list-pins","member-info","emoji-list"]` |

BEFORE core diagnostic (the exact gateway log line, captured via `defaultRuntime.error`):

```

channels.slack.accounts.broken.botToken: unresolved SecretRef "env:default:OPENCLAW_PROOF_MISSING_TOKEN".
  at resolveSlackBotToken → resolveSlackAccount → listEnabledSlackAccounts → listSlackMessageActions
  → describeSlackMessageTool → describeMessageToolSafely (src/channels/plugins/message-action-discovery.ts:110)
```

target.title: fix(synology-chat): stop fabricating send message ids
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Synology Chat outbound sends fabricated a platform message id. After the incoming-webhook `sendMessage`/`sendFileUrl` calls resolve with a bare `true` (`extensions/synology-chat/src/client.ts:96`, `:132` — `Promise<boolean>`, no id in the webhook contract), the adapter returned `messageId: \`sc-${Date.now()}\`` and stamped that synthetic id into the delivery receipt's `primaryPlatformMessageId`, `platformMessageIds`, and `parts` (`extensions/synology-chat/src/channel.ts`). Downstream consumers treat `messageId` as a real platform id (e.g. delivery-pin lookup in `src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts`), so a fabricated id can be acted on as if it were deliverable platform state. This is the same shape as the merged nostr fix #110006, which removed the synthetic `nostr-${Date.now()}` id in favor of an honest send result.

## Why This Change Was Made

The plugin-sdk contract already defines the sanctioned representation for "no platform id": the empty string sentinel. `createEmptyChannelResult` documents that "empty message ids are the legacy 'no platform id' sentinel expected by outbound callers" (`src/plugin-sdk/channel-send-result.ts:55`), and `buildChannelSendResult` normalizes a missing id to `""` (`src/plugin-sdk/channel-send-result.ts:120`). Sibling channels that receive no platform id from their transport (qqbot `extensions/qqbot/src/channel.ts:52`, googlechat `extensions/googlechat/src/channel.adapters.ts:52`) pass an empty `results` array to `createMessageReceiptFromOutboundResults`, producing a receipt with no platform ids and no parts. This change adopts exactly that shape: `messageId: ""` and a receipt built from an empty results array (keeping `threadId` = chat id for routing context only). Note the receipt builder falls back from `messageId` to `chatId` when resolving a part id (`src/channels/message/receipt.ts:17-27`), so passing the chat id alongside an empty message id would have re-laundered the chat id into a fake platform message id; the empty-results form avoids that. Downstream is safe for the sentinel: the delivery-pin path explicitly guards `if (!params.messageId)` (`src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts:1075`), and result aggregation uses truthiness (`deliver.ts:2572`, `:2618`). Scope is limited to the two send paths; no SDK or core changes.

## User Impact

Successful Synology Chat text and media sends now report an empty message id and a receipt with no platform message ids instead of a plausible-looking but fake `sc-<timestamp>` id. Delivery itself is unchanged; only the reported send metadata becomes honest. Operators relying on delivery receipts will no longer see synthetic ids that cannot be resolved on the NAS.

## Evidence

- Precedent: #110006 (merged) removed the identical `nostr-${Date.now()}` fabrication in the nostr adapter.
- Tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/synology-chat` — with the fix, `channel.test.ts` is 40 passed / 41 total, and the full plugin suite shows 120 passed with 3 failures that reproduce identically on unmodified `origin/main` (`5143d909b9`): two setup-wizard prompt failures in `core.test.ts` and `setup status honors the selected named account` in `channel.test.ts` (locale-dependent wizard prompt expectations, unrelated to this change).
- Reverse verification: with only `channel.ts` stashed, the three updated/new assertions fail (`declares message adapter durable text and media with receipt proofs`, `sendText returns an honest empty-id result on success`, `sendMedia returns an honest empty-id result on success`); with the fix restored, all three pass.
- New/updated coverage: `sendText`/`sendMedia` success tests now assert `messageId === ""`, `receipt.primaryPlatformMessageId === undefined`, empty `platformMessageIds`/`parts`, and `receipt.threadId === chatId`; the message-adapter capability proof test asserts the same honest receipt shape for both text and media.

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

target.title: fix(ui): pair tool calls with earlier-sorted orphan results in chat coalescing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

For native-runtime transcripts, Control UI tool cards render only the "Tool output" section because the stored `toolResult` message's timestamp can precede the assistant message carrying the `toolCall` block. `coalesceToolActivityMessages` scans forward only, so the result sorts before its call and the backward pairing never fires.

## Why This Change Was Made

Root cause: `buildChatItems` orders by timestamp, native transcripts can persist results before calls, and the coalesce scan was unidirectional.

The fix tracks orphaned tool results by call id (`openResultIndexes`), then iterates **every unresolved call** in the assistant message and attempts backward pairing against earlier-sorted orphan results. Multi-call messages pair each call independently — calls with a matching orphan merge backward into the orphan's timeline slot; calls without a match register forward.

target.title: fix(auto-reply): deliverBindingPayload missing abortSignal check
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin binding notifications could still be delivered via `routeReplyToOriginating`, `dispatcher.sendToolResult`, or `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` after the dispatch operation has been aborted, because `deliverBindingPayload` did not check or propagate the dispatch abort signal. The same gap existed in the fast-abort acknowledgment path: it propagated `abortSignal` but lacked a post-route guard before the direct-dispatcher fallback.

## Why This Change Was Made

`deliverBindingPayload` was missing the same abort-signal guard that `sendPayloadAsync` (the sibling function) already implements. Aligned them by adding:

1. **Pre-check**: `params.replyOptions?.abortSignal?.aborted` early return
2. **Propagation**: pass `params.replyOptions?.abortSignal` to `routeReplyToOriginating` options
3. **Post-check**: after the async `routeReplyToOriginating` call, check `.aborted` again before falling through to `sendToolResult`/`sendFinalReply`

The fast-abort acknowledgment path had the same pattern: it propagated `abortSignal` through `routeReplyToOriginating` but did not re-check after the await, so a cancellation during routed delivery could still reach `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` on the wrong surface.

Since `deliverBindingPayload` is defined inside `dispatchReplyFromConfigInner`'s closure, `params.replyOptions?.abortSignal` is directly accessible — no need for `getDispatchAbortSignal()`.

> **Key fix difference from initial approach:** `getDispatchAbortSignal()` returns the **operation signal** (from `dispatchReplyOperation`) after `ensureDispatchReplyOperation` is called, not the original `replyOptions.abortSignal`. When an external `AbortController` fires, the operation signal does not propagate the abort. Using `params.replyOptions?.abortSignal` directly guarantees the correct signal is checked in both pre-check and post-check.

## User Impact

Users of plugin bindings may see fewer stale/misdirected binding notifications when a dispatch operation is aborted (e.g. session timeout, manual cancellation). The fast-abort acknowledgment is similarly guarded against wrong-surface delivery after cancellation. No behavior change for normal (non-aborted) dispatch paths.

## Evidence

### Test results

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.acp-abort.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.reply-dispatch.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.lifecycle-and-bindings.test-utils.ts

 ✓ 3 files  →  313 tests passed (313)
```

### Lint and type checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `tsgo:core` (type) | ✅ |
| `test-types` | ✅ |
| `oxlint` | ✅ |
| `oxfmt` | ✅ |

### E2E proof: Mid-route abort with 500ms async delay (the race window)

Uses a **real HTTP server**, **real `dispatchReplyFromConfig` pipeline**, **real `AbortController`**, and a **500ms artificial delay** in `routeReply` to simulate the async race window. Everything except `routeReply` (requires a real channel gateway) is real.

```
[PROOF] HTTP server started at http://127.0.0.1:45835
[PROOF]  +0ms    Calling dispatchReplyFromConfig with non-aborted signal...
                 ↓ signal.aborted = false
[PROOF]  +258ms  routeReply invoked — starting 500ms delay
                 ↓ async await — dispatch is WAITING for routeReply
[PROOF]  +761ms  abortController.abort() fired  ← ABORT FIRES DURING AWAIT
                 ↓ signal.aborted = true
[PROOF]  +763ms  Result: {"queuedFinal":false,"counts":{"tool":0,"block":0,"final":0}}
[PROOF]  ✅ sendFinalReply NOT called  — post-check guard active
[PROOF]  ✅ sendToolResult NOT called  — post-check guard active
[PROOF]  🎯 VERDICT: Mid-route abort guard verified at +763ms
```

The 500ms delay makes the race window observable: abort fires at +761ms *during* the async `routeReplyToOriginating` await, and the post-check catches it 2ms later at +763ms, suppressing fallback delivery.

### Fast-abort post-route guard

After the `routeReplyToOriginating` await returns null, `params.replyOptions?.abortSignal?.aborted` is checked before the `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` fallback, preventing wrong-surface delivery when cancellation races with the route.

target.title: Durable Core PR 4/6: persist agent-turn front doors
target.body:
## Durable Core stack context

This is **PR 4/6**. Its incremental role is to persist seven agent-turn acceptance front doors and fence uncertain restart replay; no new schema or config.

### End state

The series targets infrastructure-level agent silence on supported OpenClaw
7.1 paths. Accepted long-running or delegated work should retain durable
identity, parent/owner attention, recovery state, and replay-safety evidence
across Gateway restart, process interruption, context overflow/compaction,
delayed children, stale claims, and ambiguous handoffs. The intended result is
truthful recovery or an explicit owner-decision/uncertainty state, not silent
loss and not blind replay.

This is not a promise that every agent will always produce a useful response.
It does not resume an arbitrary operating-system process, guarantee exactly-once
external effects, prove delivery through every transport, or replace profile,
skill, prompt, and model quality.

### Official 7.1 baseline and residual gap

Official 7.1 already has authoritative lifecycle owners for tasks and task
delivery, Task Flow runs, subagents, outbound and session delivery queues,
leases, sessions, ACP, restart/boot, conversation bindings, audit, diagnostics,
and the shared SQLite schema. This stack keeps those owners authoritative.

The residual gap appears when a fact crosses owners. No single official 7.1
owner can safely answer all of these questions without taking authority from
another owner:

- which parent, session, or owner must receive attention for accepted work;
- which task, flow, subagent, session, delivery, and generic execution facts
  refer to the same run;
- whether a handoff was accepted, consumed, owner-acknowledged, or externally
  delivered;
- whether work left running after process loss is stale, reclaimable, blocked,
  or uncertain;
- whether a possible side effect makes automatic replay unsafe;
- how an operator can inspect those facts without reading or mutating SQLite
  directly.

Durable Core therefore adds only residual cross-owner facts, owner-first
recovery coordination, and bounded inspection. It reuses `state_leases` for
attempt authority and the existing `schema_meta`/`user_version` owner for schema
versioning. It does not add a second task, flow, subagent, delivery, session, or
migration ledger.

### Root causes and stack coverage

| Root-cause family | Stack response |
|---|---|
| Accepted work exists only in process memory | PR2 persistence substrate plus PR4 durable acceptance front doors |
| Coordinator or parent can go silent after delegation | PR3 source-backed wake obligations and persistent session attention |
| Restart/interruption leaves stale or contradictory state | PR3 owner-first recovery, PR4 fenced turn settlement, PR5 expired-claim recovery |
| Handoff attempt is mistaken for consumption, ACK, or delivery | PR3 explicit proof boundaries and PR6 inspection |
| A side effect may have happened before process loss | PR4 uncertainty/replay fence and PR5 operation-specific recovery policy |
| Operators cannot explain pending or blocked work | PR6 bounded read-only Gateway/CLI projections |

### Six-PR map

| PR | Incremental role |
|---|---|
| [PR1 #107375](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/107375) | Residual-gap RFC, official 7.1 owner comparison, invariants, and compatibility plan |
| [PR2 #111121](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/111121) | Opt-in shared-state foundation with exactly ten residual tables |
| [PR3 #111278](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/111278) | Owner-first Gateway recovery and persistent session attention |
| [PR4 #111343](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/111343) | Durable agent-turn front doors, liveness, settlement, and uncertain-replay fence |
| [PR5 #111464](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/111464) | Operation-scoped worker, attempt fencing, and expired-claim recovery |
| [PR6 #111487](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/111487) | Bounded read-only Gateway and CLI inspection |

### Review model

All six PRs target `release/2026.7.1` at
`0790d9f593ad30c940ed93b5872a8cf6d6f3cf8c`, so GitHub displays a cumulative
diff for each later PR. Review and merge order remains PR1 through PR6.
Review the incremental change for this slice at [PR4-only compare](https://github.com/mjnkao/openclaw/compare/codex/durable-core-pr3-recovery-v5...codex/durable-core-pr4-agent-turn-v1).

Exact head for this PR: `456ca1b7e0118acc69c9bdaf68d88526cbf5234c`.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw 7.1 entry points can acknowledge agent work before durable evidence exists. During long tool work, Gateway restart can leave the caller with an uncertain outcome; the established CLI fallback or restart recovery can then run the same work again and risk duplicate side effects.

This slice persists admission, liveness, and settlement around existing agent-turn and `chat.send` front doors:

- channel reply and queued follow-up runners
- CLI Gateway path
- isolated cron execution
- Gateway `agent` RPC
- OpenAI-compatible HTTP streaming
- OpenResponses streaming
- `chat.send`

It reuses the PR2 durable tables and PR3 recovery/owner-attention substrate. It adds no generic executor, parallel worker, database table, or hidden environment activation path.

## Contract

- Persist intake before dispatch or success-shaped acceptance output.
- Await durable admission before the first OpenAI assistant chunk.
- Await durable admission before OpenResponses created/in-progress/output events.
- Fail closed in `authority` mode when intake cannot be persisted.
- Keep `observe` best effort and disabled mode database-free.
- Renew a 30-second heartbeat while a turn is active.
- Settle each turn through one fenced terminal path.
- Store message length and SHA-256 hash, not raw prompt text.
- Mark intake metadata-only and non-replayable.
- Refuse CLI embedded fallback after an uncertain Gateway result.
- Block main-session auto-resume while an open `lost_after_dispatch` fact exists.
- Deliver restart attention with tools disabled, including after persistent queue recovery.
- Keep explicit retry authority with the source owner.

## Evidence

### Exact-head validation

Production head `2e95463c53aa4bd025c7702634dab684d209b85c` passed:

- focused current-head matrix: 359 tests across 5 Vitest shards
- unit shard: 32 passed
- Gateway OpenAI/OpenResponses matrix: 159 passed
- infra heartbeat/system-event/session-queue shard: 96 passed
- command/fail-closed fallback shard: 37 passed
- main-session restart-recovery shard: 35 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:all`
- changed-file type-aware Oxlint
- `pnpm lint:agent:ingress-owner`
- Oxfmt on all changed files
- `git diff --check`
- production-head `pnpm build`, reporting `OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (2e95463)`

Current exact head `456ca1b7e0118acc69c9bdaf68d88526cbf5234c`, whose only additional change is that CI ratchet correction, then passed:

- plugin SDK surface regression: 9/9
- raw loopback streaming rejection proof: 3/3 Gateway projects
- `pnpm tsgo:all`
- Oxfmt and `git diff --check`
- exact-head `pnpm build`, reporting `OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (456ca1b)`

Regression coverage proves:

- OpenAI admission failure emits no assistant success chunk.
- OpenResponses admission failure emits no created, in-progress, or output event.
- Open durable side-effect uncertainty blocks main-session auto-resume.
- Restart attention preserves `disableTools=true` through the persistent queue.
- Durable attention bypasses an empty heartbeat file without exposing tools.

### Exact-head isolated restart and no-replay trace

An isolated authority-mode Gateway used channels/bindings disabled and a private loopback endpoint.

1. A normal CLI-to-Gateway turn persisted `received -> running -> succeeded`.
2. A second turn appended one line to an isolated side-effect counter, then entered a 120-second tool wait.
3. Before shutdown it remained `running/running`, recorded a heartbeat at 30,002 ms, and the side-effect count was exactly one.
4. Gateway shutdown made the waiting CLI exit non-zero with the explicit uncertain-outcome message; embedded fallback did not run.
5. Restart against the same SQLite state produced exactly one `lost/lost` turn, one open `lost_after_dispatch` fact, and one `restart_interrupted` wake.
6. The attached attention turn ran without tools and ACKed the wake in one attempt.
7. The side-effect count remained one and the transcript contained exactly one `exec` call and zero `process` calls.
8. A separate post-restart CLI turn succeeded normally.
9. A third boot changed only the Gateway startup count.

Stable counts across the third boot:

```text
lost_agent_turns=1
succeeded_agent_turns=3
uncertainty_facts=1
open_uncertainty_facts=1
wake_obligations=1
acked_wakes=1
wake_attempts=1
side_effect_count=1
transcript_exec_calls=1
```

The isolated durable database contained zero raw proof-marker occurrences in `metadata_json`; records retained bounded lengths and hashes only.

## Boundary

This PR does not claim arbitrary tool-process resumption, automatic replay from metadata-only intake, exactly-once external effects, or external-channel delivery. Durable core records uncertain effects, prevents automatic replay, and routes owner attention; reconciliation or explicit retry remains an owner decision.

This PR is AI-assisted. The implementation and proof were manually reviewed against the owner-authority, admission, recovery, replay, privacy, and disabled-mode boundaries above.

## Raw Streaming Admission Rejection Proof

A fresh exact-head proof started the real loopback Gateway HTTP handlers with both streaming front doors enabled, fault-injected rejection at the durable authority intake boundary, and captured the complete redacted SSE responses. It ran successfully in the Gateway core, server, and client Vitest projects (3/3); all produced the same frames and made zero agent dispatch calls.

```text

exact_head=456ca1b7e0118acc69c9bdaf68d88526cbf5234c
transport=real loopback HTTP through exact-head Gateway handlers
fault=fault-injected durable authority intake rejection

openai.content_type=text/event-stream; charset=utf-8
```

The OpenAI-compatible response contains no assistant role or `chat.completion.chunk`. The OpenResponses response contains no `response.created`, `response.in_progress`, or output-item event. This directly demonstrates that durable admission rejection precedes every success-shaped frame for both protocols. Volatile response IDs, timestamps, loopback port, local paths, and process identifiers are redacted; no private endpoint, token, prompt, or provider data is present.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(ollama): release failed setup response bodies before returning
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a connection leak where Ollama setup flows (`openclaw configure` / onboarding model pull, cloud auth check, and the tools-capability scan) would leave the HTTP response body unread when a `/api/me`, `/api/pull`, or `/api/show` call returned a non-OK status — or, for `/api/me`, even on success. With a slow or stalled Ollama server (or proxy in front of it), the keep-alive socket stays occupied after the call returns, pinning the connection in the dispatcher pool until GC.

## Why This Change Was Made

The repo's established contract for guarded fetches is to cancel the response body before returning on paths that do not consume it (`await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`, as in `extensions/huggingface/models.ts` and `extensions/openrouter/usage.ts`, and the merged "cancel redirect relay response body before returning" fix). The SSRF guard's `release()` only closes the dispatcher — it does not drain or cancel an unread response body — so each caller owns this. `extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` missed it at four return/throw sites (`/api/me` non-OK and success, `/api/pull` non-OK, `/api/show` non-OK). Each now cancels the body first. Out of scope: other extensions — their error paths already consume the body via `readResponseTextLimited` or cancel it explicitly.

## User Impact

Operators running Ollama setup against a slow, stalled, or misbehaving server no longer leak sockets on failed pulls/auth checks, so repeated setup attempts cannot accumulate pinned keep-alive connections. ## Why This Change Was Made

Adding `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to the `execFileSync` call ensures the `az` subprocess is forcefully terminated when the 30s timeout fires.

The async counterpart `execAzAsync` calls `runExec` (from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/process-runtime`), not the Node.js built-in `execFile`. `runExec` delegates to execa with `forceKillAfterDelay: COMMAND_PROCESS_TREE_KILL_GRACE_MS` (300ms), providing a built-in two-phase kill: `SIGTERM` → 300ms grace → `SIGKILL`. Source: `src/process/exec.ts:50-63`, `src/process/exec-spawn.ts:7`.

| **Changed surface** | `execAz` in `extensions/microsoft-foundry/cli.ts:47-58` — one line |

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

## Summary

- remove the `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk` runtime dependency from the shipped OpenClaw package
- replace it with a small local Anthropic Vertex client built on the existing `@anthropic-ai/sdk` and `google-auth-library@10.6.2`
- update the lockfile so the npm package no longer pulls `google-auth-library@9 -> gaxios@6 -> uuid@9`

## Why

`openclaw@2026.5.2-beta.1` introduced a clean npm audit regression for consumers: `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk@0.16.0` depends on `google-auth-library@^9.4.2`, which resolves to `gaxios@6.7.1` and `uuid@9.0.1`. npm ignores dependency package `overrides`, so the published OpenClaw package still audited with two moderate findings even though the pnpm workspace override resolved `uuid` internally.

## Validation

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`
- `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/anthropic-vertex`
- `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/anthropic-vertex/stream-runtime.ts`
- `pnpm audit --prod --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- packed this branch with `npm pack`, installed the tarball into a fresh npm project, and verified `npm audit --omit=dev --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- tarball install dependency tree no longer contains `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk`, `google-auth-library@9`, `gaxios@6`, or `uuid@9`
